stories.event: Abaye rode along the bank of the Sagya River while Rav Mesharshiyya and other rabbis sat on the far bank and did not stand for him.
stories.turn: Abaye challenged them for not standing before their primary teacher.
stories.outcome: They answered that they had not seen him at all.
stories.summary: Abaye was riding his donkey along the Sagya River, and Rav Mesharshiyya and other rabbis on the other bank did not rise. He asked them whether he was not their primary teacher, owed honor even from afar. They replied that they had not noticed him.

stories.actor: Ravina and Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti
stories.event: While Ravina sat before Rabbi Yirmeya, a man passed by without covering his head.
stories.turn: Ravina called the man rude.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yirmeya suggested the man was from Mata Mehasya, where rabbis are so common that people are less careful to honor them.
stories.summary: Ravina was sitting before Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti when a man walked past without covering his head. Ravina remarked on how rude he was. Rabbi Yirmeya excused him, suggesting he came from Mata Mehasya, where rabbis are commonplace.

stories.event: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak juggled three myrtle branches while dancing before brides.
stories.turn: Rabbi Zeira complained that the old man was humiliating the scholars, but at his death a pillar of fire separated him from everyone else.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Zeira conceded that the old man's branch (or folly, or method) had earned him this honor.
stories.summary: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak used to dance before brides juggling three myrtle branches, and Rabbi Zeira thought it demeaned the Sages. When Rav Shmuel died, a pillar of fire, granted to only one or two people in a generation, separated him from everyone. Rabbi Zeira then admitted that his dancing had earned him this reward.

stories.event: King Agrippa rerouted his entourage to yield before a bride's wedding procession.
stories.turn: He did so although a king is not required to yield.
stories.outcome: The Sages praised him.
stories.summary: Although a king of Israel takes precedence over a wedding procession, King Agrippa stepped aside for a bride. The Sages praised him for it.

stories.actor: A woman and the child she raised
stories.event: A woman came to Jerusalem with a child on her shoulders and raised him.
stories.turn: When grown, he had intercourse with her.
stories.outcome: They were brought to court and stoned, on the presumption that he was her son.
stories.summary: A woman arrived in Jerusalem carrying a child on her shoulders and raised him as her own. Later he had relations with her. The court stoned them both, not because he was definitely her son but because he had always clung to her as one.

stories.event: Hillel provided a formerly wealthy poor man with a horse and a servant to run before him.
stories.turn: Once no servant could be found.
stories.outcome: Hillel himself ran before the man for three mil.
stories.summary: Hillel the Elder supplied an impoverished man of noble family with a horse to ride and a servant to run ahead of him. One day no servant was available. Hillel ran ahead of him himself for three mil.

stories.actor: Rabbi Nehemya and a poor man
stories.event: A poor man who was used to fatty meat and aged wine asked Rabbi Nehemya for charity.
stories.turn: Rabbi Nehemya invited him to share his lentils, and the man died after eating them.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Nehemya lamented the man, blaming the man's own excessive indulgence.
stories.summary: A man came to Rabbi Nehemya for charity and said he usually dined on fatty meat and aged wine. Rabbi Nehemya asked him to share his own meal of lentils; the man ate and died. Rabbi Nehemya said 'Woe to this one killed by Nehemya,' meaning the man should not have pampered himself so.

stories.event: A poor man asked Rava for charity and said he ate fattened hen and aged wine.
stories.turn: When Rava rebuked him for burdening the community, the man said God provides each person's food; just then Rava's sister, unseen for thirteen years, arrived bringing fattened hen and aged wine.
stories.outcome: Rava conceded to the man and invited him to eat.
stories.summary: A man seeking charity told Rava he dined on fattened hen and aged wine, and Rava asked whether he cared about the community's burden. The man replied that he ate from God, not from them. At that moment Rava's sister, whom he had not seen for thirteen years, arrived with exactly a fattened hen and aged wine. Rava told the man he had been answered and invited him to eat.

stories.event: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi; he covered himself with boils by incantation, she healed him by magic, and he fled to a demon-haunted bathhouse.
stories.turn: He survived the night unharmed in the dangerous bathhouse.
stories.outcome: He told the Sages two imperial soldiers guarded him, and they explained that one who resists forbidden intercourse is granted a miracle.
stories.summary: A noblewoman propositioned Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi, so he used an incantation to cover himself in boils, but she healed him with magic. He fled and hid in a bathhouse so dangerous that even two people together were harmed there by day. The next day he told the Sages that two imperial guards had protected him all night, and they concluded that a miracle is done for one who escapes forbidden intercourse.

stories.event: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rabbi Tzadok, and he stalled by asking for food; she offered non-kosher food and put it in the oven.
stories.turn: He climbed into the burning oven, saying that one who commits this sin falls into fire.
stories.outcome: She said that had she known how seriously he took it she would not have troubled him.
stories.summary: When a noblewoman propositioned Rabbi Tzadok, he said he was too weak and asked for food. She offered non-kosher food and lit the oven to roast it, and he climbed into the oven, explaining that one who commits such a sin falls into fire. She told him that had she known it mattered so much, she would not have pressed him.

stories.event: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rav Kahana, a basket seller, and he excused himself to adorn himself.
stories.turn: He went up to the roof and threw himself off, and Elijah came and caught him.
stories.outcome: Elijah complained of traveling four hundred parasangs; Rav Kahana blamed poverty, and Elijah gave him a basket of dinars.
stories.summary: Rav Kahana sold baskets, and a noblewoman propositioned him. He said he would go prepare himself, climbed to the roof and jumped. Elijah the prophet caught him and complained of the four-hundred-parasang trip; Rav Kahana answered that poverty had put him in that position, and Elijah gave him a basket full of dinars.

stories.actor: A woman, Rav Nahman, Rav Anan and Mar Ukva
stories.event: A woman about to remarry deeded her property to her daughter to keep it from her new husband, then was divorced and wanted it back.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman tore up the daughter's deed, and Rav Anan complained to Mar Ukva that Rav Nahman tears up people's documents.
stories.outcome: On hearing the facts, Mar Ukva cited Shmuel's ruling that a document of evasion should be torn, vindicating Rav Nahman.
stories.summary: Before remarrying, a woman wrote her property over to her daughter to shield it from her husband; after she was divorced, she wanted it back. Rav Nahman tore the deed. Rav Anan went to Mar Ukva to complain about 'Nahman the farmer' destroying documents, but when Mar Ukva heard the details he cited Shmuel: a document of evasion is to be torn.

stories.event: A man deposited seven pearls wrapped in a sheet with Rabbi Meyasha, who died without leaving instructions.
stories.turn: The depositor and the heirs disputed ownership before Rabbi Ami.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Ami awarded the pearls to the depositor, since Rabbi Meyasha was not wealthy and the depositor gave an identifying mark.
stories.summary: A man left seven pearls tied in a sheet at the house of Rabbi Meyasha, grandson of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who then died without saying whose they were. The parties came before Rabbi Ami. He ruled for the claimant, because Rabbi Meyasha could not have afforded such pearls and the claimant identified them by a sign.

stories.event: A man deposited a silver goblet with Hasa, who died without instructions.
stories.turn: The case came before Rav Nahman.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman awarded it to the depositor, since Hasa was not wealthy and the depositor gave an identifying mark.
stories.summary: A man deposited a silver goblet with Hasa, who died without leaving word about it. Rav Nahman heard the case. He gave the goblet to the claimant, noting that Hasa was not wealthy and that the claimant could identify it.

stories.event: A man deposited silk with Rav Dimi, brother of Rav Safra, who died without instructions.
stories.turn: The case came before Rabbi Abba.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Abba awarded the silk to the depositor, since Rav Dimi was not wealthy and the depositor gave an identifying mark.
stories.summary: A man deposited silk with Rav Dimi, who died without saying whose it was. Rabbi Abba heard the dispute. He ruled for the claimant, since Rav Dimi was not wealthy and the claimant gave a distinguishing mark.

stories.event: A dying man said his property should go to Toviya.
stories.turn: After his death a Toviya came to claim it.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan ruled that Toviya had come and could take it.
stories.summary: A man on his deathbed left his property to 'Toviya' and then died. A man named Toviya arrived to claim it. Rabbi Yohanan ruled that this Toviya was the heir, with no concern that another Toviya was meant.

stories.event: Ravin went as agent to betroth a woman to his son.
stories.turn: Her family refused the son, so Ravin betrothed her to himself without informing his son.
stories.outcome: He married her himself, fearing someone else would betroth her in the meantime.
stories.summary: Ravin the Pious went to arrange his son's betrothal to a woman, but ended up betrothing her to himself. Her family would not give her to the son, only to the father. He did not first tell his son, fearing another suitor would take her meanwhile.

stories.actor: Rav and Rabba bar bar Hana
stories.event: Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy a certain field for him.
stories.turn: Rav bought it for himself instead, because the violent locals would sell to Rav but not to Rabba bar bar Hana.
stories.outcome: Rav kept the land, acting without informing him lest someone else buy it first.
stories.summary: Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy a field for him, and Rav bought it for himself. The field lay in a valley of violent men who respected Rav but not Rabba bar bar Hana. Rav did not stop to tell him, fearing another buyer would take it in the meantime.

stories.event: Rabbi Abba bought a field Rav Giddel was negotiating for, and Rav Giddel complained up the chain to Rav Yitzhak Nappaha.
stories.turn: Confronted at the Festival, Rabbi Abba said he had not known, and refused to sell his first land but offered it as a gift.
stories.outcome: Rav Giddel would not accept a gift and Rabbi Abba would not use it, so it became known as 'the land of the Sages'.
stories.summary: Rav Giddel was negotiating for a field when Rabbi Abba bought it; Rav Giddel complained to Rabbi Zeira, who took it to Rav Yitzhak Nappaha. At the Festival Rav Yitzhak asked Rabbi Abba about a pauper whose loaf is snatched, and Rabbi Abba agreed the snatcher is wicked, said he had not known, and offered the land as a gift since he would not sell his first purchase. Rav Giddel refused gifts and Rabbi Abba would not use it, so neither took the field and it was called the land of the Sages.

stories.event: Returning home after many years, he recognized his daughter by hearing her called by name at the river and followed her home.
stories.turn: His wife saw him suddenly and died of the shock.
stories.outcome: He prayed for her and she was revived.
stories.summary: Sitting by the river, Rabbi Hananya heard a girl called 'daughter of Hakhinai' and realized she was his own daughter, so he followed her home. His wife, sifting flour, looked up, saw him, and died from the shock. He protested to God that this could not be her reward, prayed for mercy, and she lived.

stories.event: After twelve years in the study hall, Rabbi Hama went first to his hometown study hall rather than surprising his wife, and a sharp young scholar questioned him.
stories.turn: He regretted that he had no such son, then stood up for the young man at home, not realizing it was his own son Oshaya.
stories.outcome: His wife asked whether a father stands for his son, revealing the truth.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hama bar Bisa studied away for twelve years and, to avoid what happened to ben Hakhinai, sent word home from the local study hall. A brilliant young man questioned him, and Rabbi Hama lamented that had he been home he could have had a son like that. When the young man followed him home and Rabbi Hama rose before him, his wife asked whether a father stands before his son: it was his son, Rabbi Oshaya.

stories.event: The daughter of ben Kalba Savua betrothed herself to his shepherd Akiva on condition he study, and her father disowned her by vow.
stories.turn: Akiva studied twenty-four years, returned with twenty-four thousand students, and honored her before all; her father came seeking release from his vow.
stories.outcome: Learning the great man was Akiva, ben Kalba Savua bowed to him and gave him half his wealth.
stories.summary: Ben Kalba Savua's daughter saw the shepherd Akiva's worth, betrothed herself to him in secret and sent him to study; her father threw her out and vowed she would get nothing of his. Akiva studied twelve years, overheard her say she would wish him to study twelve more, and did so, returning with twenty-four thousand students; when she fell at his feet he told his students that all their learning was hers. Her father, coming to the great sage to annul his vow, said he would never have vowed had he thought Akiva would learn anything, and on learning who he was fell at his feet and gave him half his wealth. Akiva's daughter later did the same for ben Azzai.

stories.event: Rav Yosef, sent to study for six years, left after three to visit his wife on Yom Kippur eve.
stories.turn: His father came out armed to meet him and rebuked him for remembering his wife.
stories.outcome: The quarrel kept them both from eating the meal before the fast.
stories.summary: Rava sent his son Rav Yosef to study for six years, but after three years, on the eve of Yom Kippur, the son set out to visit his wife. Rava took a weapon and went to meet him, asking scornfully whether he had remembered his woman. In the quarrel, neither of them ate the final meal before the fast.

stories.event: Ravina held wine belonging to his orphaned nephew and was taking his own wine to Sikhra to sell.
stories.turn: He asked Rav Ashi whether he could take the orphan's wine along.
stories.outcome: Rav Ashi told him to go, since the orphan's wine was no better than his own.
stories.summary: Ravina was looking after wine belonging to his orphaned nephew, Ravina the younger, and was taking his own wine to sell in Sikhra. He asked Rav Ashi whether he could bring the orphan's wine too. Rav Ashi told him to go ahead, since the orphan's wine deserved no better treatment than his own.

stories.actor: Rava and a divorced betrothed couple
stories.event: A betrothed couple who had divorced came before Rava for a money judgment.
stories.turn: Rava placed an intermediary between them, and Rav Adda bar Mattana objected citing the rule that betrothed parties may deal directly.
stories.outcome: Rava answered that this couple were plainly familiar with each other; another version reverses who proposed and who objected.
stories.summary: A divorced betrothed man and woman came before Rava, with Rav Adda bar Mattana present. Rava put an intermediary between them, and Rav Adda objected that, by a teaching in Evel Rabbati, betrothed people need no go-between. Rava replied that he could see these two were familiar with each other; in another version Rav Adda urged the intermediary and gave that reply himself.

stories.event: A man bowed and kissed Rabbi Yonatan's foot in front of Rabbi Hanina.
stories.turn: Rabbi Hanina asked why, and Rabbi Yonatan explained that the man had signed his property over to his sons.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yonatan had forced the sons to support him, which earned his gratitude.
stories.summary: While Rabbi Hanina and Rabbi Yonatan stood together, a man bent down and kissed Rabbi Yonatan's foot. Rabbi Hanina asked what it meant. Rabbi Yonatan said the man had written his property over to his sons and he had compelled them to feed him.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yeshevav (or a certain man) and his friend
stories.event: A man sought to give more than a fifth of his property to charity.
stories.turn: His friend stepped in.
stories.outcome: The friend did not let him; it was either Rabbi Yeshevav stopping someone, or Rabbi Akiva stopping Rabbi Yeshevav.
stories.summary: Someone wanted to give away more than a fifth of his property to charity, and his friend would not allow it. In one version the friend was Rabbi Yeshevav; in another, Rabbi Yeshevav was the giver and Rabbi Akiva stopped him.

stories.event: A man told Rabbi Ami that another had presumptive status as a priest because he read first from the Torah.
stories.turn: Rabbi Ami asked whether that was as a priest or as a great man, and the witness said a Levite read after him.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Ami elevated the man to the priesthood on his word.
stories.summary: A man testified to Rabbi Ami that someone was a presumed priest because he was called first to the Torah. Rabbi Ami asked whether that might be because he was a prominent man, and the witness answered that a Levite read after him. Rabbi Ami confirmed his priesthood on that testimony.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and a witness
stories.event: A man told Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that another was a presumed Levite because he read second from the Torah.
stories.turn: Asked whether that was as a Levite or as a great man, the witness said a priest read before him.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi confirmed him as a Levite on his word.
stories.summary: A man testified before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that someone was a Levite because he read second in synagogue. The rabbi asked whether he might simply be prominent, and the witness said a priest had read first. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi then established him as a Levite.

stories.event: When a witness claimed someone was a priest for reading first, Reish Lakish demanded proof he received teruma at the threshing floor, and Rabbi Elazar asked whether priesthood ends where there is no threshing floor.
stories.turn: Later the same case came before Rabbi Yohanan, who gave Rabbi Elazar's exact answer.
stories.outcome: Reish Lakish glared at Rabbi Elazar for citing Rabbi Yohanan's words without naming him.
stories.summary: Reish Lakish insisted that a priest's status be proven by his share of teruma at the threshing floor, and Rabbi Elazar retorted that priesthood cannot depend on there being a threshing floor. Later, sitting before Rabbi Yohanan, a similar case arose and Rabbi Yohanan gave the same retort. Reish Lakish looked harshly at Rabbi Elazar and rebuked him for repeating Rabbi Yohanan's teaching without attributing it, since he would have accepted it then.
